lesson.title: Reversing the Cotangent Rule: The Integral of csc^2(x)
lesson.summary: The derivative of cot(x) is -csc^2(x), so running that fact backward makes the integral of csc^2(x) equal to -cot(x), not cot(x).
lesson.body:
The integral of csc^2(x) is: integral of csc^2(x) dx = -cot(x) + C.

This follows from the derivative of cotangent: the derivative of cot(x) is -csc^2(x). To turn that into an integral rule, differentiate the candidate answer -cot(x) and check what happens. The derivative of -cot(x) is -(-csc^2(x)), which simplifies to csc^2(x). Since differentiating -cot(x) produces exactly csc^2(x), -cot(x) is an antiderivative of csc^2(x), which is the rule stated above.

The negative sign here follows the same pattern noted in earlier chapters: cotangent is a co- function, and co- functions carry negative signs in their derivatives. That negative sign has to be canceled by negating cot(x) itself when building the antiderivative, which is exactly why the integral of csc^2(x) is -cot(x) and not cot(x). This mirrors the relationship between sin(x) and cos(x) from earlier in the unit, and it contrasts with the previous chapter, where integral of sec^2(x) dx = tan(x) + C needed no sign flip, since tangent is not a co- function.

Worked example: find integral of 3*csc^2(x) dx. Pull out the constant: 3 * integral of csc^2(x) dx = 3*(-cot(x)) + C = -3*cot(x) + C. Verify by differentiating: the derivative of -3*cot(x) is -3*(-csc^2(x)) = 3*csc^2(x), which matches the original integrand.

As with the tangent and secant squared pair, keep the domain in mind: csc(x) and cot(x) are both undefined wherever sin(x) = 0, at integer multiples of pi. The rule integral of csc^2(x) dx = -cot(x) + C is valid on any interval avoiding those points.
